short: Finland held off a Soviet invasion for 105 days and kept its independence.
full:
Having secured a free hand in the Baltic, Stalin demanded Finnish territory near Leningrad and, when it was refused, invaded on 30 November 1939 with around 450,000 men. The Finnish army was a fraction of that size and had almost no tanks or aircraft, but it was trained for forest fighting in deep snow. Ski troops cut Soviet columns confined to the few roads into pockets, called motti, and destroyed them piecemeal, most completely at Suomussalmi. The sniper Simo Hayha was credited with over 500 kills.

The Red Army, its officer corps gutted by the purges, lost perhaps 130,000 to 200,000 dead against Finland's 26,000. In February 1940 it changed method, massing artillery against the Mannerheim Line on the Karelian Isthmus and grinding through by weight of shell. Finland accepted terms on 13 March, ceding about a tenth of its territory but remaining independent. The Soviet showing persuaded Hitler that the Soviet Union could be beaten quickly, a conclusion he acted on the following year.
